procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 17, 1966 of the Punjab High Court (Circuit Bench) Delhi in Criminal Appeal No. 63-D of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant took the matter in appeal to the Punjab High Court. The High Court maintained the conviction of the appellant under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and s. 161, Indian Penal Code and also the sentence to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years awarded to the appellant on each count. The High Court, however, set aside the order with regard to the payment of fine or imprisonment in default.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Shiv Raj Singh, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave after the Punjab High Court affirmed his conviction. He challenged the validity of the sanction order for his prosecution, arguing that all relevant materials were not placed before the sanctioning authority.

issue.issue_text: Whether the order of sanction fulfilled the requirements of s. 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

facts: The appellant argued that the sanction to prosecute was invalid because not all relevant materials were placed before the sanctioning authority, the D.I.G. Police.
The order of sanction itself stated the facts that constituted the alleged offense.
The order also contained a recital that the D.I.G., after having "fully and carefully" examined the material before him, considered that a prima facie case was made out against the appellant.
law: Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act requires a valid sanction from a competent authority for the prosecution of a public servant.

A sanction is not valid if it is merely a formality or is given without the sanctioning authority applying its mind to the facts of the case. A sanction that is too brief or "cryptic" may be insufficient.
application: The Court examined the contents of the sanction order directly.
It found that, on its face, the order was not cryptic. It detailed the facts of the offense and explicitly stated that the sanctioning authority had fully and carefully examined the material.
The Court considered this recital in the order as sufficient evidence that the D.I.G. had applied his mind to the case.
The Court distinguished this case from a precedent cited by the appellant (*Gokulchand v. The King*), stating that the sanction in that case was "much more cryptic and materially different."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the order of sanction was valid because it showed on its face the facts constituting the offense and recited that the sanctioning authority had fully and carefully examined the material. Therefore, the order fulfilled the requirements of Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

issue.issue_text: When a public servant is charged under s. 161 I.P.C. for taking illegal gratification for an official act, is it necessary for the court to consider whether the public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act?

facts: A police officer (the appellant) accused individuals of disposing of an illegitimate child and demanded a bribe to refrain from prosecuting them.
The appellant received the bribe money in a trap set by the anti-corruption department.
The appellant's defense was that concealing the birth of an illegitimate child was not actually a criminal offense.
Therefore, he argued, he was not capable of performing the official act (prosecution) for which he took the bribe, and thus could not be guilty under s. 161 I.P.C.
law: Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.) criminalizes a public servant taking illegal gratification for doing or forbearing to do an official act.
The Court cited its previous decision in 'Mahesh Prasad v. The State of Uttar Pradesh' as a binding precedent on this issue.
application: The Supreme Court directly rejected the appellant's argument.

It held that when a public servant is charged under s. 161 I.P.C., the court does not need to examine whether the public servant was actually capable of doing the official act, or even if they intended to do it.

The Court stated that the offense is committed when the illegal gratification is taken for the purpose of doing or procuring an official act, regardless of whether that act is possible or was ever intended.
The Court explicitly followed its earlier ruling in 'Mahesh Prasad v. The State of Uttar Pradesh' to reach this conclusion.

As a separate point, the Court also found that the appellant's actions constituted an offense under s. 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, as he had grossly abused his position as a public servant to obtain a pecuniary advantage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that for a conviction under s. 161 I.P.C., it is not necessary for the court to consider whether the public servant was actually capable of or intended to perform the official act for which the bribe was taken. The mere act of taking the illegal gratification in connection with their official duties is sufficient to constitute the offense.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was guilty of abusing his position as a public servant under s. 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

facts: The appellant, a police officer, accused individuals of disposing of an illegitimate child and demanded a bribe to refrain from prosecuting them.
The appellant was caught in a trap and the bribe money was recovered from him.
The High Court found these facts to be proven.
law: Section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act states that a public servant commits criminal misconduct if he, by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as a public servant, obtains for himself any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage.
application: The Court considered the appellant's argument that since the concealment of an illegitimate child was not a real offense, taking money to refrain from an 'imaginary prosecution' was not a crime.
The Court rejected this argument, stating that regardless of the validity of the threatened prosecution, the appellant's actions constituted a gross abuse of his position as a police officer.
The Court found that by using his official capacity to extort money, the appellant had abused his position to obtain a pecuniary advantage for himself.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that based on the proven facts, there was no doubt that the appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a public servant within the meaning of s. 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, and the charge under that section was established.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed on the appellant was excessive.

facts: The appellant was a police officer.
The High Court found that the appellant had grossly abused his position to extort money and a gold ring from citizens.
law: A police officer, in their official capacity, is expected to maintain a high standard of integrity and uphold the law.
application: The court noted that the proven facts showed a gross abuse of the appellant's official position.
The appellant's actions were a direct contradiction of the high standard of integrity expected of him as a police officer.
reasoning.conclusion: Based on the circumstances, particularly the appellant's gross abuse of his position as a police officer, the Supreme Court was satisfied that the sentence imposed was not excessive and rejected the appellant's contention.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the order of sanction fulfilled the requirements of s. 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
appellant_arguments: The order of sanction was legally invalid because all relevant papers and materials were not placed before the sanctioning authority.
The appellant cited the case of Gokulchand v. The King, where a sanction that merely named the person and the alleged contravention was deemed insufficient.
A prosecution witness (P.W. 9) could not confirm which specific documents were sent to the sanctioning authority as they were in a sealed cover.
respondent_arguments: The order of sanction was valid and fulfilled all legal requirements.
The order itself showed on its face the facts constituting the offence and that a prima facie case was made out.
The order explicitly stated that the sanctioning authority had 'fully and carefully' examined the material before him.
The precedent cited by the appellant (Gokulchand v. The King) was not applicable as the sanction order in that case was much more cryptic and materially different.

arguments.issue_text: When a public servant is charged under s. 161 I.P.C. for taking illegal gratification for an official act, is it necessary for the court to consider whether the public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act?
appellant_arguments: The act for which the bribe was allegedly taken (prosecuting for concealment of an illegitimate child's birth) was not a real offence, so the appellant was not capable of performing the official act in question.
Obtaining money to refrain from an 'imaginary prosecution' cannot be considered an offence under s. 161 I.P.C.
respondent_arguments: It is not necessary for the court to determine if the public servant was actually capable of doing, or intended to do, the official act for which the bribe was taken.
This principle is supported by the precedent set in Mahesh Prasad v. The State of Uttar Pradesh.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was guilty of abusing his position as a public servant under s. 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was not guilty because the act he was forbearing from (prosecution) was related to a non-existent crime, and therefore obtaining money for it does not constitute an abuse of position under the Act.
respondent_arguments: The facts proven in the High Court established that the appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a public servant.
By his actions, the appellant obtained a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for himself, which satisfies the requirements of s. 5(1)(d).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed on the appellant was excessive.
respondent_arguments: The sentence was not excessive and was appropriate for the crime committed.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order of sanction is valid under Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act if it shows on its face the facts that constitute the offence and that the sanctioning authority, after fully and carefully examining the material, was satisfied that a prima facie case existed.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the sanction for prosecution was valid as it was sufficient on its face, and that a public servant is guilty of taking illegal gratification regardless of whether they were actually capable of performing the official act for which the bribe was taken. Based on the facts established by the High Court, the appellant's actions of obtaining money constituted a gross abuse of his position as a public servant, thereby justifying the conviction under both s. 161 I.P.C. and s. 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
legal_tests_applied: For a sanction to be valid under s. 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, the order must show on its face the facts constituting the offence and that the sanctioning authority examined the material to establish a prima facie case.

When a public servant is charged under s. 161 I.P.C. for taking illegal gratification for an official act, it is not necessary for the court to consider whether the public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act.

A public servant is guilty of criminal misconduct under s. 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act if, by abusing their position, they obtain for themselves any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the challenge to the sanction order because the order itself recited the facts of the offence and stated that the sanctioning authority had 'fully and carefully' examined the material, distinguishing it from the 'much more cryptic' order in the precedent cited by the appellant.

The appellant's argument that he could not be guilty because the threatened prosecution was for a non-existent crime was dismissed, as the court held that the public servant's actual capability to perform the official act is irrelevant to a charge under s. 161 I.P.C.

The court found that the facts proven by the High Court were sufficient to establish that the appellant had grossly abused his position as a public servant to obtain a pecuniary advantage, fulfilling the requirements for a conviction under s. 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
The court summarily concluded, without providing detailed reasoning, that the sentence imposed was not excessive.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position on the sanction's validity was upheld because the court found the order was self-sufficient, showing on its face the facts of the offence and the application of mind by the sanctioning authority.

The court accepted the respondent's legal argument, supported by the precedent in 'Mahesh Prasad v. The State of Uttar Pradesh', that the capability of the public servant to perform the act for which a bribe is taken is not a necessary element of the offence under s. 161 I.P.C.
The court agreed with the respondent that the facts established in the lower court proved the appellant had abused his position to obtain a pecuniary advantage, satisfying the elements of s. 5(1)(d).
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning is strictly legal and does not explicitly state any public policy considerations.
